newsitem.title: USA: Two California thrifts merge in $200 million deal.
newsitem.headline: Two California thrifts merge in $200 million deal.

text.p: The California thrift industry shrank further Monday as Golden State Bancorp Inc. and Cenfed Financial Corp. became the region's latest savings and loans to merge in a stock swap valued at around $200 million.
Under terms of the deal, Golden State, parent of Glendale Federal Bank (Glenfed), will offer 1.2 shares of its stock for each Pasadena, Calif.-based Cenfed share in a tax-free pooling of interests.

"This transaction will enhance Golden State shareholder value in several ways," said Stephen Trafton, chairman and chief executive officer of Golden State. The deal would immediately boost earnings and increase Golden State's return on equity by more than 80 basis points, he said.
Golden State, based in Glendale, Calif., expects to record pretax charges of about $30 million in conjunction with the merger.
Despite the projected benefits, the stock of both thrifts fell Monday. Golden State slipped 50 cents to $28.19 on the New York Stock Exchange, and Cenfed dropped 62.5 cents to $33.375 on Nasdaq.

Analysts cited shareholders' concerns that the merger, which requires issuance of more than 7 million new shares, would dilute the benefits they hope to reap from a potential multibillion-dollar award in a lawsuit by Glenfed against the federal government.

Glenfed has filed claims worth $2 billion against the federal government for changes the institution said were made to accounting rules offered as "goodwill" incentives for thrifts to buy other troubled thrifts during the savings and loan crisis of the 1980s.

Hoping to take advantage of the goodwill incentives, Glenfed in 1981 acquired a troubled Florida thrift with $734 million in losses. Changes to certain accounting rules saddled Glenfed and a number of other thrifts with large losses of their own.
Richard Fink, vice chairman of Golden State, told Reuters the merger would reduce shareholders' prospective gains from any damages won in the lawsuit by about 10 percent.

"If we were to receive our full claim we might receive $2 billion, which would equate to close $15 a share. But there's a lot of uncertainty with any trial and the money couldn't be received for a couple of years," Fink said.

Fink said Golden State had decided it would be wiser to take advantage of the current strength in its stock, which has benefited from speculation about the goodwill claim, toward a strategic acquisition.
Fink also said Golden State is on the lookout for further acquisitions.

Golden State said some jobs will be eliminated and some branches closed as a result of its merger with Cenfed, but no further details were provided. Golden State has 2,256 full-time employees and Cenfed has about 400 full- and part-time employees.
The latest California thrift merger comes on the heels of Washington Mutual Inc.'s $8 billion acquisition of Great Western Financial Corp., which was completed early July.

"I think the California S&L consolidation will continue and the growing scarcity of thrifts will continue to boost the stocks' values," said Thomas O'Donnell, analyst with Smith Barney. "This deal was somewhat of a defensive maneuver or unintended poison pill for Golden State."
The merged company will have assets of $18.5 billion, deposits of $10.9 billion and 193 banking offices.
The transaction is expected to close in early 1998. Tad Lowrey, president and chief executive officer of Cenfed, will join both boards of directors.
Cenfed's board terminated the 5 percent stock repurchase program that was announced in January 1997.
